content: The study evaluates the efficacy and safety of Tixagevimab and Cilgavimab, monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), in comparison to a placebo for the treatment of COVID-19 in outpatient settings. The following are the detailed findings: 1. All-Cause Mortality: The analysis included 452 participants in the experimental group and 451 in the control group. The risk ratio (RR) for all-cause mortality was 1.00 (95% CI: 0.32 to 3.07), indicating no significant difference between the monoclonal antibody group and the placebo group. The test for overall effect yielded a Z-score of 0.00 with a p-value of 1.00, suggesting no statistical significance. There was no heterogeneity observed in this analysis. 2. Hospitalization or Hospital Visit: The experimental group consisted of 413 participants, while the control group had 421 participants. The risk ratio for hospitalization or hospital visits was 0.43 (95% CI: 0.25 to 0.75), favoring the monoclonal antibody group. The test for overall effect showed a Z-score of 2.98 with a p-value of 0.003, indicating a statistically significant reduction in hospitalizations or hospital visits in the monoclonal antibody group. No heterogeneity was detected in this analysis. 3. Admission to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU): The experimental group included 413 participants, and the control group had 421 participants. The risk ratio for ICU admission was 0.28 (95% CI: 0.08 to 0.99), favoring the monoclonal antibody group. The test for overall effect yielded a Z-score of 1.98 with a p-value of 0.05, indicating borderline statistical significance. No heterogeneity was observed in this analysis. 4. Serious Adverse Events: The experimental group had 452 participants, while the control group included 451 participants. The risk ratio for serious adverse events was 0.61 (95% CI: 0.40 to 0.92), favoring the monoclonal antibody group. The test for overall effect showed a Z-score of 2.35 with a p-value of 0.02, indicating a statistically significant reduction in serious adverse events in the monoclonal antibody group. No heterogeneity was detected in this analysis. Risk of Bias Assessment: The study demonstrated low risk of bias across all domains, including random sequence generation (selection bias), allocation concealment (selection bias), blinding of participants and personnel (performance bias), blinding of outcome assessment (detection bias), incomplete outcome data (attrition bias), and selective reporting (reporting bias). Conclusion: The use of Tixagevimab and Cilgavimab in outpatient settings for COVID-19 was associated with a statistically significant reduction in hospitalization or hospital visits, ICU admissions (borderline significance), and serious adverse events. However, no significant difference was observed in all-cause mortality. The study was conducted with a low risk of bias, ensuring the reliability of the findings.
